stem: A trading platform has an RTO of 30 minutes. Which recovery site is appropriate?

options.text: A hot site
options.why: Only a hot site, with hardware, software and current data already running, can restore service inside 30 minutes.

options.text: A warm site
options.why: A warm site has the equipment but not current data. Restoring and validating it takes hours at best.

options.text: A cold site
options.why: A cold site is space, power and connectivity. Standing it up takes days or weeks.

options.text: An offsite backup vault
options.why: Storing media offsite protects the data. It provides nowhere to run the platform.

stem: A charity can tolerate several days of downtime and has a very limited budget. Which recovery option fits?

options.text: A cold site
options.why: With a tolerant RTO and a tight budget, paying only for space, power and connectivity is the appropriate trade.

options.text: A hot site
options.why: A hot site is the most expensive option by a wide margin, and the RTO does not require it.

options.text: A warm site
options.why: Reasonable in the middle of the range, and it still means paying to keep hardware and software standing by.

options.text: Clustering across two data centres
options.why: That is a high availability design, the most expensive approach of all, for an organisation that can accept days of downtime.

stem: A database must continue serving requests with its session state intact if one node fails. Which design meets this?

options.text: Clustering, so the nodes act as one logical system sharing state
options.why: Clustering is defined by shared state and workload takeover, which is what preserving sessions across a node failure requires.

options.text: A load balancer distributing connections across independent nodes
options.why: Load balancing spreads requests and the nodes do not share state, so the sessions on the failed node are lost.

options.text: Replication to a standby copy
options.why: Replication keeps a second copy current. On its own it does not provide automatic takeover with live session state.

options.text: Nightly backups to a second data centre
options.why: Backups restore data eventually. They provide no continuity at all.

stem: A web farm is struggling under traffic growth. Requests must be spread across all available servers. Which device is required?

options.text: A load balancer
options.why: Distributing incoming requests across a pool of servers for capacity is exactly what a load balancer does.

options.text: A cluster manager
options.why: Clustering makes servers act as one logical system with shared state, which is not what spreading stateless web requests needs.

options.text: A jump server
options.why: A jump server is a controlled entry point for administrators, not a traffic distributor.

options.text: A forward proxy
options.why: A forward proxy handles internal users going out to the internet, the opposite direction.

stem: A company replicates its file server continuously to a second data centre. Ransomware encrypts the primary. What happens?

options.text: The encrypted files replicate to the secondary, so both copies are unusable
options.why: Replication faithfully copies every change, including malicious ones. It protects against hardware and site failure, not against corruption.

options.text: The secondary is unaffected because replication is one way
options.why: One way is the direction of the copy, which is exactly why the encryption travels from primary to secondary.

options.text: The secondary retains previous versions and can be rolled back
options.why: That is versioned backup or snapshot behaviour. Plain replication keeps only the current state.

options.text: Replication halts automatically when corruption is detected
options.why: Replication does not evaluate whether changes are legitimate. It has no idea the file was encrypted rather than edited.

stem: A transaction system must be recoverable to any moment, not just to the last backup. Which method supports this?

options.text: Journaling every change so the log can be replayed to a chosen point
options.why: A change journal allows point in time recovery at very fine granularity, which is how a near zero RPO is achieved.

options.text: Hourly snapshots
options.why: Snapshots give you the hourly points, and nothing between them.

options.text: Nightly full backups
options.why: That gives you one recovery point per day, which is an RPO of up to 24 hours.

options.text: Continuous replication to a standby
options.why: Replication gives you the current state at the standby. It does not let you choose an earlier moment.

stem: A data centre must experience no interruption at all during a mains failure and must stay running for at least 48 hours. What is required?

options.text: A UPS and a generator together
options.why: The UPS carries the load instantly through the seconds the generator needs to start, and the generator sustains the site for as long as there is fuel.

options.text: A generator alone
options.why: A generator has a start delay. Without a UPS, everything drops for those seconds, which violates 'no interruption at all'.

options.text: A UPS alone, sized for 48 hours
options.why: Battery capacity at data centre load is measured in minutes. Sizing one for 48 hours is not practical.

options.text: Dual mains feeds from the same substation
options.why: Two feeds from one substation share its failure. It is not a substitute for local generation.

stem: A retailer must validate its disaster recovery plan before the holiday season without any impact on production. Which test is appropriate?

options.text: A tabletop exercise
options.why: Participants talk through the plan in a room. It has no production impact, which the requirement demands.

options.text: A full failover test to the recovery site
options.why: The most conclusive test and the most disruptive. The stem forbids production impact.

options.text: A parallel processing test
options.why: Lower impact than failover and still brings up recovery systems alongside production, so it is not zero impact.

options.text: A simulation with systems partially engaged
options.why: Simulations touch systems and carry some risk. Discussion only means tabletop.

stem: Which test provides the strongest evidence that the recovery site can genuinely carry production load?

options.text: A full failover test with production cut over to the recovery site
options.why: Only actually running production at the recovery site proves it can. Everything else is inference.

options.text: A tabletop exercise attended by all system owners
options.why: Discussion validates the plan on paper and proves nothing about the systems.

options.text: A walkthrough of the runbooks with the operations team
options.why: A walkthrough checks the procedure is complete and correct, not that the infrastructure works.

options.text: Reviewing the recovery site's capacity documentation
options.why: Documentation review is the weakest form of assurance available.

stem: A company's backups were encrypted by ransomware along with production. Which TWO design properties would have preserved a usable copy? (Choose two.)

options.text: An offline copy the production systems cannot reach
options.why: Ransomware can only encrypt what the compromised host can write to. An air-gapped copy is out of reach.

options.text: Immutable storage where written objects cannot be altered for a retention period
options.why: Even with credentials, the attacker cannot overwrite an object under an immutability lock.

options.text: Continuous replication to a second data centre
options.why: Replication copies the encryption as faithfully as it copies the data. It protects against site loss, not corruption.

options.text: Encrypting the backup files at rest
options.why: That protects their confidentiality. The ransomware encrypts them again regardless.

options.text: Running the backup job twice as often
options.why: More frequent copies to a reachable share means more encrypted copies.

stem: A critical service runs on six identical load-balanced servers with the same operating system, same version and same configuration. A single vendor advisory takes all six offline simultaneously. Which design principle was missing?

options.text: Platform diversity, so a flaw common to one platform cannot affect every node at once
options.why: Redundancy protects against one instance failing independently. Six identical nodes share every flaw, so a common vulnerability is a single point of failure wearing a disguise.

options.text: More redundancy: a seventh identical server
options.why: A seventh copy of the same thing fails for the same reason at the same moment.

options.text: Geographic dispersion across two sites
options.why: That protects against a site-level event. A software flaw travels to the second site unchanged.

options.text: A warm recovery site
options.why: A recovery site is for restoring after a disaster. It does not stop a fleet-wide flaw, and a warm site built identically inherits it.

stem: An organisation moves to a multi-cloud design across two providers. Which risk does this address, and which does it not?

options.text: It addresses a single provider's outage or regional failure; it does not address the organisation's own misconfiguration, which can be replicated to both
options.why: Provider independence is the benefit. Your own identity and configuration mistakes travel with you, and most cloud incidents are customer misconfigurations.

options.text: It addresses misconfiguration risk, because two providers validate each other
options.why: Providers do not review your configuration. Nothing cross-checks the two deployments unless you build it.

options.text: It addresses all availability risk, removing the need for backups
options.why: Availability design does not replace backups. Deleted or corrupted data replicates to both providers promptly.

options.text: It addresses nothing, since both providers run the same hardware
options.why: Independent control planes, operations teams and failure domains are the point, whatever the hardware underneath.

stem: A disaster recovery plan is tested successfully. During a real incident six months later it stalls because the only engineer who knows the failover procedure is on leave and unreachable. Which aspect of capacity planning failed?

options.text: People: there was no trained cover for a role the plan depended on
options.why: Capacity planning covers people as well as kit. A plan with a single point of human failure has not been planned for capacity, however well the technology performs.

options.text: Technology: the failover systems were insufficient
options.why: The stem says the test succeeded, so the technology was adequate.

options.text: Infrastructure: power and cooling at the recovery site
options.why: Nothing indicates a facility constraint.

options.text: The plan should have been tested more frequently
options.why: More testing with the same single engineer reproduces the same dependency.

stem: A secondary site holds enough servers to carry full production load, but its electrical supply and cooling are sized for 40% of it. What has been overlooked?

options.text: Infrastructure capacity: power, cooling and space must carry the load the technology is sized for
options.why: Servers that cannot be powered or cooled are inventory. Infrastructure is named separately precisely because it is assessed separately and often forgotten.

options.text: Technology capacity
options.why: The compute is correctly sized. The constraint sits beneath it.

options.text: People capacity
options.why: No staffing constraint is described.

options.text: The site should be reclassified as cold rather than warm
options.why: Site classification describes readiness of equipment and data, not whether the facility can power what is installed.

stem: A business states it can tolerate losing at most one hour of transactions. Backups currently run nightly at 23:00. What must change, and which metric is being expressed?

options.text: Backup frequency must increase to hourly or continuous; the stated tolerance is the recovery point objective
options.why: RPO is how much data loss is acceptable, and backup frequency is what sets it. A nightly schedule can lose up to twenty-four hours.

options.text: Recovery speed must improve; the tolerance is the recovery time objective
options.why: RTO is how long until service returns. The stem talks about lost transactions, which is data, so it is RPO.

options.text: Retention must be extended so older copies are available
options.why: Retention is how far back you can go. It does not reduce the gap since the last copy.

options.text: Backups must be encrypted to protect the lost transactions
options.why: Encryption addresses disclosure. The requirement here is about how much work disappears.

stem: Offsite backup media are transported by a third-party courier to a storage facility. Which control most directly limits the impact if a cartridge is lost in transit?

options.text: Encrypting the backup media, with keys held separately from the media
options.why: Once media leaves your control, encryption is the remaining control. Keys travelling with the cartridge would defeat it, which is why separation is part of the answer.

options.text: Increasing backup frequency
options.why: That reduces potential data loss and does nothing about a copy in someone else's hands.

options.text: Using a courier with better insurance
options.why: Insurance transfers financial loss. It does not prevent disclosure or a notification obligation.

options.text: Keeping an additional onsite copy
options.why: Helps availability, and the lost cartridge remains readable by whoever has it.

stem: A team has run nightly backups for two years and has never performed a restore. What is the correct characterisation of their position?

options.text: They have an untested hypothesis: until a restore succeeds, there is no evidence the backups are usable or that recovery fits the RTO
options.why: Backup jobs reporting success routinely produce unreadable or incomplete sets. Recovery testing is the only thing that converts a backup into a control.

options.text: They are adequately protected, since the jobs report success
options.why: A successful job means the software finished. It does not mean the output can be restored.

options.text: They need snapshots in addition, which do not require testing
options.why: Snapshots need testing too, and typically share storage with production, so they do not survive what takes the array or the site.

options.text: They should increase retention before testing anything
options.why: Keeping more unverified copies for longer multiplies the hypothesis rather than testing it.

stem: An organisation wants to validate its incident response under realistic pressure, with responders using actual tooling against an injected scenario, without taking production down. Which exercise type fits?

options.text: A simulation
options.why: A simulation runs a realistic scenario with real tooling and real decisions, sitting between a discussion-based tabletop and an actual failover that moves production.

options.text: A tabletop exercise
options.why: A tabletop is discussion-based around a table. Nobody touches tooling, which is what the stem asks for.

options.text: A failover test
options.why: A failover test actually moves production to the secondary, which the stem rules out.

options.text: A penetration test
options.why: That assesses technical exploitability, not the response process.

stem: Which TWO statements about resilience design are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Redundant identical systems share every flaw those systems have, so diversity addresses a risk redundancy cannot
options.why: A common vulnerability across a fleet is a single point of failure however many instances exist.

options.text: Continuity of operations planning covers people and facilities, not only technology
options.why: Capacity planning is split across people, technology and infrastructure for exactly this reason.

options.text: A multi-cloud design removes the risk of customer misconfiguration
options.why: Your configuration errors replicate to every provider you deploy to.

options.text: Snapshots stored on the production array are an adequate substitute for offsite backups
options.why: They do not survive loss of the array, the site, or ransomware that can reach the storage.

options.text: Platform diversity reduces operational complexity
options.why: It increases it. More platforms means more expertise, patching and ways to misconfigure, which is the trade being made.

stem: During a brief 8 second mains dip, which device keeps equipment running with no interruption?

options.text: The UPS
options.why: A UPS carries the load instantly from battery, which is what covers short dips and bridges to a generator during longer outages.

options.text: The generator
options.why: A generator needs time to start and stabilise. For an 8 second dip it would barely have begun.

options.text: Dual power supplies in each server
options.why: Redundant supplies protect against a failed supply unit. If both feeds lose mains power, both go down.

options.text: Power distribution units with surge protection
options.why: Surge protection handles voltage spikes. It stores no energy to carry a loss of supply.

stem: During a failover test the recovery site's servers start correctly, but the backup software refuses to run because its licences are tied to the primary site's hardware. Which dimension of capacity planning was missed?

options.text: Infrastructure
options.why: Power, cooling, space and network were all adequate; the servers started. The shortfall was in what the software is licensed to do.

options.text: People
options.why: Nobody was missing or untrained. The software itself refused to run.

options.text: The site should have been a hot site rather than a warm one
options.why: A hot site with the same licensing gap would fail the same way. The type of site is not the problem.

options.text: Technology: the licences must cover the recovery site as well as the hardware
options.why: Licences are part of technology capacity. Servers that start but cannot run the software are not capacity.

stem: A server room has a generator that starts automatically 20 seconds after mains power fails, and no UPS. What happens to the servers during a five minute outage?

options.text: They lose power for about 20 seconds, until the generator takes over
options.why: A generator needs time to start. Without a UPS to bridge those seconds, the servers go down and restart.

options.text: Nothing; the generator engages with no gap
options.why: Generators engage after a start delay. Covering that gap with no interruption is exactly what a UPS is for.

options.text: They run without interruption until the generator's fuel runs out
options.why: The interruption happens at the start, before the generator is running, not at the end.

options.text: They stay up, because dual power supplies in each server bridge the gap
options.why: Dual supplies protect against one supply or feed failing. Both are fed by the same failed mains until the generator starts.
